newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FEATURE - HK's displaced seek new haven in Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - HK's displaced seek new haven in Taiwan.

text.p: In 1986, paroled political prisoner "Lao Kuang" swam a day and a half from China to Hong Kong, seeking sanctuary in the freewheeling British colony.
Last July, he left Hong Kong for a new haven -- Taiwan.

"I tied myself to six basketballs and swam 35 hours to reach Hong Kong. I was lucky I wasn't caught and thought I would spend the rest of my life in Hong Kong," he said, asking to be referred to by the nickname "Lao Kuang" instead of his real name.
Lao Kuang, now 50, is a chef in a Taipei Cantonese restaurant.

Imprisoned as a "reactionary" during China's chaotic 1966-76 Cultural Revolution, he is one of many former mainlanders to pull up stakes again for Taiwan as the July 1 handover of Hong Kong approaches.

Chou Ching-chun opened his private Hong Kong and Macau Institute in Taipei in 1994 to promote the rights of displaced emigrants from Hong Kong and Macau, the Portuguese territory that reverts to Chinese rule in 1999.
Chou said he knows what it's like to be a political refugee: "I am one of them. It's just that I moved here 13 years ago."

Chou, who fled communist China for Hong Kong in 1961, said he sought refuge in Taiwan soon after Beijing and London signed the 1984 Joint Declaration outlining Hong Kong's 1997 return to the motherland after more than 150 years as a British colony.
"As soon as I learned that British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher had signed the agreement, I decided to move to Taiwan, where I can speak the language," Chou told Reuters.
Chou said he worried that his long advocacy of democracy in Hong Kong would earn him a post-handover prison term.
"I was afraid they would try to get even with me because of my pro-democracy campaign in Hong Kong in the 1980s," he said.
Chou said many of the 30,000 Hong Kong and Macanese people now living in Taiwan considered the Nationalist-ruled island a sanctuary for freedom after the handover.
There are strong indications that many people still in Hong Kong and Macau feel the same.

About 16,000 Hong Kong and Macau people have applied to the Overseas Chinese Affairs Commission for "overseas Chinese certificates", which are needed to enter Taiwan -- and which are seen by many as assisting possible flight after the handover.
Yet there are no guarantees.
Taiwan itself is reluctant to open its doors to a flood of Hong Kong refugees, something it fears could disrupt social order and further strain its already difficult mainland relations.
Taipei's exiled Republic of China, like Beijing's arch-rival People's Republic, regards Hong Kong as Chinese territory and its people as Chinese subjects.
The territory's shift to Beijing's rule has prompted Taipei to begin redrawing the lines.

The Interior Ministry has drafted stricter registration rules for Hong Kong and Macau people living, working and even visiting Taiwan -- sparking howls of protest from emigres. "It is unfair," said Chan Wing-sing, a co-owner of another Taipei Cantonese restaurant. "We decided to move to Taiwan because we believe that we would be treated as equals to local people as the Nationalist government has said again and again."
On the most fundamental level, Taiwan's own future remains clouded by its long and bitter rivalry with China -- something that emigres from Hong Kong are quick to point out.
"The communists can sack Taiwan easily. The question is only whether they want to," said Michael Chung, who runs a Taipei centre dedicated to the Chinese mystic belief qigong.
"Given the military might of the mainland, whose missiles could reach anywhere on the island, Taiwan could last no more than three days before it surrenders," he said.

Beijing, which has viewed Nationalist-ruled Taiwan as a rebel-held province since a 1949 civil war split them, has said that after the return of Hong Kong and Macau, Taiwan would be all that remained to be "reunified with the motherland".
Beijing also maintains a standing threat to retake Taiwan by force if it strays from its official policy of eventual reunification and embarks on a "splittist" course toward full independence.
Asked where he would go if Beijing were to take aggressive or even military steps to take Taiwan back, qigong practitioner Chung spoke with a mix of resignation and practicality.
"I would go back to Hong Kong -- because it is a good place to make money," he said.
